phishing: Phishing is when attackers impersonate people or services to steal info. Never click unfamiliar links, verify sender addresses, and avoid sharing sensitive data.
If a message asks for passwords, codes, or payments, treat it as suspicious. Contact the company using an official channel to verify.
Quick check: Does the message create urgency, ask for money, or contain strange URLs? These are common phishing signs.
passwords: Use long, unique passwords for every account. Aim for at least 12 characters with a mix of letters, numbers, and symbols.
A password manager (e.g., Bitwarden) can generate and store strong passwords so you don’t have to remember them.
If one account is breached, change that password everywhere it was reused and enable two-factor authentication.
two_factor_auth: Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for all important accounts; prefer app-based authenticators over SMS for stronger security.
If you must use SMS 2FA, combine it with strong passwords and consider registering recovery keys or backup codes safely.
Authenticator apps: Google Authenticator, Authy, and FreeOTP are common options. Store backup codes in a secure place.
malware_and_virus: If you suspect malware: disconnect from the internet, run a reputable anti-malware scan, and avoid entering any credentials until the device is clean.
Keep backups of important files offline or in a secure cloud with versioning; this helps recover from malicious encryption (ransomware).
For Windows, use Defender or Malwarebytes for scanning; on Android, uninstall suspicious apps and check app permissions.
ransomware: If files are encrypted and a ransom is demanded, do not pay without guidance from authorities — payment doesn't guarantee recovery.
Isolate the affected device, preserve logs, and contact local cybercrime authorities and your organization’s IT/security team.
Restore from backups after confirming backups are not infected. Consider professional incident response help for large incidents.
sim_swap: SIM-swap fraud occurs when attackers transfer your number to a new SIM to intercept codes. Contact your carrier immediately if you lose signal unexpectedly.
Ask your mobile provider to add a PIN or security lock on your account and avoid sharing identity details publicly.
Use app-based authenticators or hardware tokens for important accounts to reduce reliance on SMS codes.
suspicious_link: Don't click the link. Instead, hover to inspect the URL (on desktop) or long-press to preview on mobile. If unsure, open the official site directly.
If you clicked a suspicious link, disconnect from the network, run a malware scan, and change passwords from a known-good device.
social_engineering: Social engineering tricks people rather than systems. Attackers may pose as coworkers, support staff, or family members asking for sensitive actions.
Verify identity using a separate channel (call the official number) before acting on requests for money, credentials, or access.
identity_theft: If you suspect identity theft, freeze your credit where applicable, report to local authorities, and notify businesses where fraud occurred.
Collect evidence (emails, messages), change passwords, and monitor bank/card statements for unauthorized transactions.
secure_browsing: Use HTTPS (lock icon) when submitting sensitive information in websites. Keep your browser and extensions updated.
Consider browser extensions like uBlock Origin and HTTPS Everywhere; review extensions periodically and remove ones you don't trust.
public_wifi: Avoid accessing banking or sensitive accounts on public Wi-Fi. Use a trusted VPN if you must connect on untrusted networks.
If you connect to public Wi-Fi, prefer sites with HTTPS and avoid file sharing or remote desktop sessions.
vpn: A VPN encrypts your network traffic between your device and the VPN server. Use a reputable provider and avoid free services that may log data.
Be aware that a VPN protects your network path but not malicious sites or compromised devices. Combine VPN with good endpoint security.
backup_and_recovery: Keep regular backups using the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 offsite (or cloud). Test restores periodically.
Maintain backups that are immutable or versioned to protect against accidental deletion or ransomware.
app_permissions: Review app permissions and remove ones that request unnecessary access (e.g., a flashlight app requesting contacts).
On mobile, restrict background access and remove apps you don't use. Keep OS and apps updated.
banking_fraud: If you notice unauthorized banking transactions, contact your bank immediately to dispute charges and secure your accounts.
Change login credentials, enable 2FA, and consider placing alerts for large transactions on your account.
reporting_scams: Report scams to your local consumer protection agency, your bank, and the mobile carrier. Preserve the original messages as evidence.
Many countries have dedicated cybercrime or anti-fraud reporting portals — file a report and follow their guidance.
iot_security: Change default device passwords on routers, cameras, and other IoT devices. Keep firmware updated and isolate IoT on a separate network when possible.
Disable remote admin features you don't need and monitor devices for unusual traffic.
children_online_safety: Use parental controls and talk to children about not sharing personal information or accepting friend requests from strangers.
Limit screen time, review app permissions, and teach children how to report inappropriate or suspicious contacts.
email_security: Be cautious with attachments from unknown senders; scan them with antivirus before opening. Verify sender addresses closely (look for typos).
Use email providers with strong spam filters and enable advanced phishing protections where available.
browser_hijack_and_ads: If your browser redirects often or shows unwanted ads, check for malicious extensions and clear browser data; run an anti-malware scan.
Reset browser settings and reinstall from the official source if problems persist.
device_theft: If a device is stolen, change passwords for accounts logged in on the device, enable remote wipe (if available), and report theft to police.
Revoke device access from account security pages (Google, Apple, Microsoft) and alert your bank if sensitive apps were present.
account_recovery: Use official account recovery flows and provide requested evidence; avoid recovery links received via messages unless they come from verified sources.
Set up recovery emails and phone numbers that you control and keep them updated.
oauth_and_third_party_apps: Review third-party apps that have access to your accounts and revoke access to apps you don't recognize.
Prefer granular permissions and avoid granting full account access unless necessary.
credentials_leak: If your credentials are leaked, change the affected password immediately, enable 2FA, and check other accounts for reuse.
Use https://haveibeenpwned.com to quickly check if your email appears in known breaches and follow their remediation guidance.
